evidence.supportingExcerpt: Lead time is the interval between defined earlier and later detection events. Lead-time bias occurs when that timing difference is mistaken for a better outcome. In a fictional course, detection at year 4 and death at year 6 gives two years from diagnosis. Moving detection to year 3 with death still at year 6 gives three recorded years without adding life. Similarly, labelling post-treatment recurrence at a blood signal before imaging confirmation can mechanically lengthen survival measured from recurrence. Align the endpoint, qualifying event and clock origin. Ten months of detection lead time is not ten added months of life. Earlier effective intervention could help, but its benefit needs separate evidence; correcting the clock alone does not solve selection, confounding or missing follow-up.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A monitoring strategy includes its schedule, positive-result rule and resulting action. Comparing that strategy with a meaningful alternative from a common origin, such as randomisation, can assess clinical outcomes and harms. Counting all assigned participants avoids selecting only those with detectable earlier signals. Analysis must also address when groups entered, how follow-up ended, whether positive tests triggered extra imaging and whether people without prior detection were omitted. c-TRAK TN tested a specific blood-surveillance and intervention design; its detection and feasibility findings do not establish a beneficial intervention window for every early signal. A fictional contrast of median survival of 24 months after blood detection versus 18 after imaging detection, without a common-origin comparison, cannot show that testing saves lives. Some or all of the difference could arise from the earlier clock or other group differences.
